introduction: The Principles of Business School-Based Assessment is a research project in which you investigate a business or industry, or develop and present a business idea of your own, following the stages of a business plan. The folder presents your research, findings and a justified conclusion; marks are given for the quality of the research, the analysis and use of business concepts, the presentation and the recommendation. Check the current CSEC syllabus and your teacher's guidance for the exact project type, length and mark allocation required.

tasks.title: Purpose of the study
tasks.explanation: State the aim of the research, the business or industry being studied and the specific questions to be answered, and describe the methods used to gather information.

tasks.title: Profile of the business
tasks.explanation: Describe the type of business, form of ownership, sector, size, location, product or service, and its importance to the local community and the economy.

tasks.title: Presentation of findings
tasks.explanation: Present the information gathered under the chosen headings - for example marketing, production, finance, and human resources - using tables, graphs and quotations from interviews.

tasks.title: Application of business concepts
tasks.explanation: Analyse the findings using the concepts and terms of the syllabus, identifying strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats, and explaining the effects on the business.

tasks.title: Justified conclusion
tasks.explanation: Draw conclusions that answer the aim of the study, make practical recommendations with reasons, and evaluate how reliable and complete your evidence was.

tasks.title: Structure and references
tasks.explanation: Present the project with a title page, table of contents, headings, page numbers, references and a bibliography, in clear accurate language and within the required length.

sampleTitle: An investigation into the marketing strategy of a small bakery in a Jamaican town

sample.body: The bakery employs eight workers and operates as a sole trader. Turnover in the last financial year was $4.8 million, of which bread accounted for 62 per cent, pastries 26 per cent and cakes 12 per cent. A questionnaire of 40 customers showed that 78 per cent buy bread daily, that price was the most important factor for 45 per cent and freshness for 37 per cent, and that 60 per cent said they would use a delivery service if one existed. Two competitors trade within 1.5 km; both sell at a lower price, but both are more than 20 minutes' walk from the school gate.
sample.tips: Present numbers in a table or graph as well as in words, and always state the source of each finding.

sample.body: Applying the marketing mix, the bakery's product and place are strong - fresh bread sold at the school gate at break time - while price is higher than the two competitors and promotion is limited to word of mouth and a signboard. This matches the Boston matrix position of a cash cow: a mature product with a high local share and little growth unless new segments are added. The distribution channel is entirely direct, which protects the margin but limits coverage. Weak promotion is the largest gap: 60 per cent of customers want delivery, which is demand for a new level of distribution rather than a lower price, and the fixed costs of the bakery mean that a price cut would reduce profit faster than the extra volume would replace it.
sample.tips: Name the concepts you use - marketing mix, cash cow, channel of distribution - and quantify the effect wherever you can.

marking: Marks reward a clear aim and appropriate research methods, a thorough description of the business, well presented findings, correct use of business concepts in the analysis, a justified conclusion and recommendations, and a neatly structured and referenced project.
checklist: Findings presented in tables, graphs or charts
SWOT or another analytical framework used
Title page, contents, page numbers and bibliography included

completedSample.title: A complete, full-mark Principles of Business SBA research project: an investigation into the marketing strategy of a small bakery, every figure computed from the shop's own sales record, a 60-customer survey, a price check and a four-week promotion trial (business, town, records and customers invented)
completedSample.viewOnlyNote: For viewing and learning only. This is an original worked example written for CSEC Compass, not a real candidate's submission and not a CXC exemplar. Marigold Bakery, the town of Fairhaven, the owner, the staff, the competitors, the 60 customers, the sales record, the interviews and the promotion trial are all INVENTED for teaching: no such business exists and no real firm's figures are shown. What is real is the method - how the aim is narrowed into research questions, how a sample and an instrument are described, how every table and percentage is computed from one set of records, how contribution, the contribution ratio, the break-even point and the margin of safety are worked out, and how a promotion is judged by whether it paid for itself. Study how the figures are derived and how the analysis admits what a small survey and one firm's own records cannot prove, then write your own project about your own chosen business. This sample cannot be copied.

categories.comment: One aim, cut into four research questions that the evidence can actually answer, so the project never drifts into a general description of bakeries. The method section names the population and the sample (60 customers, selected at the shop door and at the transport centre on four different days and at three different times), the four instruments - the bakery's own sales record, a 13-item customer questionnaire (ten closed questions and three ratings), three interviews and a price check - and what each instrument can and cannot show. The limitations are stated before the data is presented, not apologised for afterwards.

The business is described in the terms the syllabus uses: type of business (a manufacturer and retailer of perishable food), form of ownership and its consequences as a sole proprietorship, the sector and the linkages to agriculture and to the distributive trades, the size (five workers, annual revenue of J$21,460,000 and one rented shop with one old van), the location and why it matters, the five product lines with their prices, and the part the bakery plays in the local economy - buying flour locally, employing five families and supplying the transport centre and two schools.

Five tables and two charts in this section, every figure computed from one of four records and none of them invented twice over: the twelve-month sales record by product and by month, the product mix with each line's share of revenue and contribution, the answers of all 60 customers to seven questions, the three rating questions with their means out of five, the four-item price check against two competitors with the percentage differences worked out, and the four-week promotion trial shown as contribution earned against the same fortnight with no promotion. Every table is labelled, the units and the period are given, and the two small cells (11 cake orders in the slowest month, and the four customers whose main purchase is a cake) are flagged as too small to read.

The findings are read through the syllabus rather than summarised: the marketing mix element by element (product, price, place, promotion), then a SWOT drawn from the evidence with each entry traced to a table, then the two promotions judged by whether they paid for themselves, then the figures a lender or the owner would need - contribution per unit, the contribution ratio, the break-even revenue and the margin of safety. The demand curve shows up where it should: the price cut sold a quarter more patties and still lost J$25,750, while the longer hours earned J$11,000 more in a fortnight without touching a price. Effects on the business are stated in money, not in adjectives.

The conclusion answers the aim in the terms the aim was set, and separates what the evidence supports from what it merely suggests. Five recommendations follow, each with the reason drawn from a named table, the cost, the person who would carry it out and the figure that would show it working within two terms. The recommendations are ranked by what they cost and what they earn, so the owner could start on Monday with the flyer and the evening hours and leave the delivery service until the order-and-collect trial has been counted.

A title page, a contents page with page numbers, numbered headings, thirteen labelled tables with their sources noted, page numbers throughout, a reference list and a bibliography, and the instruments printed in full in the appendix. Language is plain and accurate, the tables are rectangular and readable in black and white, and the appendix carries the questionnaire and the interview schedule so a marker can check any figure back to the instrument that produced it.

pages.heading: Title page, contents and note on sources
pages.body:
An investigation into the marketing strategy of a small bakery in a Jamaican town. The business studied is Marigold Bakery of Market Street, Fairhaven, a sole proprietorship employing five people, and the study covers the twelve months of its last financial year (July to June) plus a four-week promotion trial in the following months.

The folder follows the six sections of the CSEC Compass Principles of Business guide in order, so each section can be marked against its own row of the Task Breakdown. Marigold Bakery, the town, the owner, the staff, the competitors and the 60 customers are invented for teaching and are labelled as such wherever they appear; the method, the arithmetic and the reasoning are the transferable part.
bullets: Section 1 - Aim and Method: the aim, the four research questions, the instruments and the limits (pages 2-4).
Section 2 - Business Description: ownership, sector, size, location, products and place in the local economy (pages 5-7).
Section 3 - Research Findings: the sales record, the customer survey, the interviews and the promotion trial (pages 8-13).
Section 4 - Analysis and Discussion: the marketing mix, the SWOT, the promotions judged by their arithmetic and the break-even (pages 14-18).
Section 5 - Conclusion and Recommendation: the aim answered, then five recommendations with reasons and costs (pages 19-20).
Section 6 - Presentation: references, bibliography and the instruments in the appendix (pages 21-22).

pages.heading: Aim and Method: the aim and the four research questions
pages.body:
The aim of this project is to find out how well the marketing of Marigold Bakery is working and what the owner should change. 'Working well' is given a meaning that can be measured: marketing is working if the bakery is reaching enough customers at a price that covers its costs and earns a contribution, and if what customers say they want matches what the shop offers.

The aim is cut into four research questions, because a single broad aim cannot be answered by one survey and is the commonest reason a project ends up describing a business instead of investigating it. Each question names the evidence that will settle it, and where the question is about money the evidence is the bakery's own records rather than anybody's opinion.

table.caption: The four research questions and the evidence each one needs
rows: 1. What does the bakery sell, to whom, and how much?
The product mix, the customers and the pattern of sales across twelve months
The bakery's own sales record for the year, by product and by month
2. How do customers find out about the bakery, and what would make them buy more?
The promotion and place elements of the mix, from the customers' side
A survey of 60 customers at the shop and the transport centre
3. How does the bakery's marketing compare with its two nearest competitors?
Price and promotion against the alternatives the customer actually has
A four-item price check on one morning, plus three interviews
4. Which marketing change would be worth the money it costs?
Whether a promotion earns more contribution than it costs
A four-week trial of two promotions against a fortnight with no promotion

pages.heading: Aim and Method: the instruments, the sample and the timetable
pages.body:
Four instruments were used, and each was chosen because the others cannot do its job. The sales record is the only source that can show what was actually sold rather than what people remember buying. The questionnaire measures the customers' own view of promotion and place. The interviews and the price check give the competitor side, which no customer survey can supply. The trial is the only instrument that can test whether a change pays for itself, because it compares two periods at the same shop under the same management.

The sample is 60 customers, taken at the shop door on four different days (two weekdays, one Saturday and one Sunday) and at three different times (7-9 a.m., 11 a.m.-2 p.m. and 4-6 p.m.), with every fourth adult who left the shop asked and one customer per household. Customers at the transport centre two streets away were added on the Saturday so that the sample is not only people who already buy at the bakery - although, as the limitations admit, an unknown number of the people who walk past and never enter are missing from every survey of this kind.

columns: What it can and cannot show

Week 2: the questionnaire drafted, tried on six customers outside the shop and rewritten where a question was misunderstood.
Weeks 3-4: the baseline fortnight and the questionnaire survey.
Weeks 5-6: the price promotion trial - patties at two for 500 - with flyers.
Weeks 7-8: the evening-opening trial with flyers and no price change.
Weeks 9-10: the price check, the three interviews and the arithmetic written up.

pages.heading: Aim and Method: the limits of this evidence
pages.body:
Four limits are stated before the findings, so that no reader has to discover them later. First, the sales record is the firm's own, and a firm records what goes through its till; waste, give-aways and unsold stock do not appear, so it measures sales rather than production. Second, 60 customers is a small sample and the people who never enter the shop are not in it, so the survey describes the bakery's own customers well and the whole town poorly. Third, the promotion trial ran for only two weeks per change, so the figures show the immediate effect and cannot show whether customers kept the new habit. Fourth, the owner and the supplier were interviewed knowing that the project was about the bakery, so their answers are interested answers; they are reported as quotations with the speaker named, never as neutral fact.

Two further limits belong to the arithmetic rather than the collecting. The competitor volumes used for the market share are estimates from the price check and the interviews, not audited figures, and the market share is therefore printed with the word 'estimated' beside it. And the break-even calculation assumes the mix of products stays as it was in the twelve months studied, which the June surge in cake orders shows is not quite true from month to month.
bullets: The sales record measures sales, not production: waste and give-aways never reach the till.
60 customers, mostly existing customers: strong about the shop, weak about the town.
Two weeks per promotion: the immediate effect is measured, the lasting habit is not.
The owner and the supplier knew the purpose of the study: interested views, quoted and named.
Competitor volumes are estimates from interviews: market share is labelled estimated.
Break-even assumes a constant product mix; the June cake surge shows the mix moves.

pages.heading: Business Description: the business, the owner and the form of ownership
pages.body:
Marigold Bakery is a small manufacturing and retail business: it bakes on the premises and sells through its own shop counter, with a short delivery round to two schools and the transport centre. It is a sole proprietorship owned by Mrs Ionie Clarke, who opened it in 2019 after eleven years working as a baker for someone else, and who is both the owner and the working head of production.

The form of ownership shapes everything else in this report. As a sole proprietor Mrs Clarke keeps all the profit after tax - about J$1.43M in the year studied - and makes every decision herself, including the prices and the promotions this project tests, which is why one interview with her could explain the whole marketing policy. Against that, she carries unlimited liability, so the shop and the van are hers personally as well as the business's, and she has no partner to share the cost of the second oven the June cake orders now need.

table.caption: Profile of the business
rows: Marigold Bakery, 14 Market Street, Fairhaven (invented town), Jamaica
A small manufacturer (baking on the premises) that also retails directly to the public
Sole proprietorship, owned and managed by Mrs Ionie Clarke since 2019
Secondary sector producing food, linked backwards to agriculture (flour, sugar, shortening) and forwards to distributive trades (schools, the transport centre, two shops)
Five workers: the owner, three full-time staff and one Saturday helper; annual revenue J$21,460,000; one rented shop and one delivery van (12 years old)
Hard dough bread, spice buns, beef patties, coconut drops and celebration cakes to order
Households within walking distance, commuters at the transport centre, two schools and small shops that resell
Employer of five families, buyer from local suppliers, supplier to the schools and the transport centre, and a place where a hot patty is sold on credit on a Friday evening

pages.heading: Business Description: what the shop sells, at what price, and the costs behind it
pages.body:
The five product lines are not equally important and the marketing has to treat them differently. Bread is the line everybody buys daily and the reason most customers come at all, so it is priced closest to the market; the celebration cakes carry the largest contribution per order but arrive only when a family has a reason to celebrate, which is why the June figures are so much larger than the rest of the year. The prices below are the shelf prices for the year studied, and the variable cost per unit is what it costs in flour, shortening, filling and packaging to make and sell one more unit - the figure that matters when a promotion is being judged.

The monthly fixed costs are what the shop costs whether it bakes one loaf or none: they come to J$460,000 a month, or J$5,520,000 for the year. Set beside the contribution the shop earned (J$6,905,550), they leave a profit of J$1,385,550 for the year, which is what makes the recommendations in this report worth carrying out: a change that adds J$11,000 a fortnight is small in the whole, but it is nearly half a month's rent.

table.caption: Monthly fixed costs of running the shop
rows: Rent of the shop on Market Street
Gas and electricity for the oven and the cold room
Wages: three full-time staff and one Saturday helper
Licences, insurance and other running costs

pages.heading: Business Description: the local market and the two competitors
pages.body:
A bakery does not price in an empty market. Within walking distance of Market Street there are two other places where a customer can buy the same four items, and the price check made on one weekday morning shows where Marigold sits between them: the larger bakery by the highway charges more and sells more variety, and the snackette by the market sells the impulse items cheaper than anybody.

The comparison explains the mixed rating the customers gave to price. On bread - the daily purchase - Marigold is the cheapest of the three, and its bread customers are the most loyal. On patties it is dearer than both, and the survey shows price dissatisfaction concentrated among the customers who buy patties at mid-morning. The competitor volumes used later for the market share are estimates taken from the interviews, and they are labelled as estimates wherever they are used.

table.caption: Price check: what the same four items cost at the three sellers
rows: A two-pound celebration cake, plain iced

bullets: Within walking distance two other places sell the same four items: the highway bakery (larger, more variety, dearer on every item) and the snackette by the market (cheapest on the impulse lines).
Estimated volumes from the interviews, labelled as such: the highway bakery about 26,000 loaves a month and the snackette about 9,000, against Marigold's 19,045 a year (INVENTED).
Marigold's estimated share of the local bread market of about 35.2% is therefore an order of magnitude, not a measurement.

pages.heading: Research findings and results: the bakery's sales record for twelve months
pages.body:
This is the evidence the whole project rests on: what the till and the order book recorded in the twelve months from July to June, by product line and by month. Revenue is units multiplied by the shelf price, so the table can be checked line by line against the prices above.

Three things are visible immediately. The year grew: J$1,673,000 in July became J$2,034,000 in June, an increase of 21.6% over twelve months, and the growth came from more units rather than from higher prices, since no price changed during the year. The slowest month was February, when the shop took J$1,602,000, which is what the owner expected after the Christmas spending and before the school term got going. And the biggest month was June at J$2,034,000, driven by the celebration cakes: 26 orders against 12 in July.

table.caption: Units sold and revenue earned, by month (July to June)

pages.heading: Research findings and results: the product mix and what each line contributes
pages.body: Revenue tells a manager what came in; contribution tells her what a line is worth after paying for what went into it. The two rankings are not the same, and the difference is the first finding of the study. Bread is 39.9% of revenue and 33.1% of contribution, so the daily line carries the shop. Patties are less than a quarter of revenue but earn the second-largest share of contribution because more of their price is left after materials. Cakes bring in only 5.8% of revenue but the highest contribution per order by far at J$2,300, which is why the June surge moves the month.

table.caption: Product mix: units, revenue, share and contribution for the year

pages.heading: Research findings and results: what the sixty customers said
pages.body: The questionnaire was answered by 60 customers over four days and three times of day. Every question below records how many of the 60 chose each answer and what share of the sample that is, so the columns add to 60 and the percentages add to 100. Two answers matter more than the rest: more than four customers in ten named word of mouth as the way they found the shop, which means the shop is barely using promotion at all; and the single most frequent answer to what would make people buy more often was not price but the hours, with 45.0% of the sample asking for later opening.

pages.heading: Research findings and results: how customers rate quality, price and service
pages.body: Three questions asked customers to score the shop out of five, and the mean of each is the figure a business would follow from month to month. Quality scored 4.37 out of 5 and service 4.43, both strongly positive; value for money scored 3.42, and it is the only one whose distribution has a heavy middle and a tail of dissatisfied answers. Freedom from a high mean is not the same as being good at everything: seven customers scored value for money at 2 and two scored it at 1, and those nine answers are the ones the price check explains, since Marigold is the cheapest on bread but the dearest on patties.

pages.heading: Research findings and results: the interviews and the price the customers face
pages.body:
The three interviews were held to explain the numbers rather than to add new ones, and each speaker is named so that her interest in the answer can be weighed. Mrs Clarke was asked directly why she does not advertise: she said that the shop has always sold out of bread by midday, so there seemed to be nothing to advertise for, and that she had never worked out what a flyer campaign would cost against what it would earn - which is exactly the calculation the trial performs. The flour supplier's representative said that Marigold buys about 40 bags of flour a month against the highway bakery's 90, and that the price he charges both is the same, so the difference between the two businesses is volume rather than buying power.

The shop assistant gave the finding no table can show: the last hour before closing is when customers ask for bread that has already been sold, and the shop turns away 'ten or twelve people a evening' in her words. That single sentence, an interested view from an employee, is the reason the evening-opening trial was designed the way it was.
bullets: Owner (Mrs Ionie Clarke, invented): has never advertised, has never costed a campaign, and prices bread to match the snackette because bread is what brings people in.
Supplier (representative of the flour distributor, invented): Marigold buys about 40 bags of flour a month against the highway bakery's 90, at the same price per bag.
Shop assistant (invented): the last hour before closing turns away 'ten or twelve people a evening' who want bread already sold out.
Price check: on bread Marigold charges J$450 against J$480 and J$430; on patties it charges J$300 against J$280 and J$250.
Interview estimate used with a label: the highway bakery sells about 26,000 loaves a month and the snackette about 9,000, against Marigold's 19,045 a year (estimated, INVENTED).

pages.heading: Research findings and results: the four-week promotion trial
pages.body:
The trial is the part of the project that turns an opinion into a figure. Three successive fortnights were recorded from the till: weeks 3-4 with no promotion, weeks 5-6 with patties at two for 500 and flyers, and weeks 7-8 with the shop open until 7 p.m. and flyers. Nothing else changed - the same staff, the same recipes and the same prices on every other line.

The price promotion worked as a price cut always works if the arithmetic is not done: it sold 25.0% more patties (750 against 600 in the fortnight) and still reduced contribution, because each patty brought in J$55 instead of J$105. The evening opening sold 10.0% more bread (770 against 700) without touching any price, and it paid for itself. The two results side by side are the most useful page in this folder, because they show that a busy shop can be a poorer shop.

pages.heading: Research findings and results: the two charts and how they were drawn
pages.body:
Two charts carry the findings, both drawn from the figures already tabulated. The first is a line chart of monthly revenue across the twelve months: revenue on the vertical axis from zero to J$2,100,000 in steps of J$300,000, the twelve months along the horizontal axis, and a single line through the twelve monthly totals from J$1,673,000 in July to J$2,034,000 in June, dipping to J$1,602,000 in February. The axis starts at zero rather than at J$1,500,000, because a cut axis would turn a fall of 10.2% into what looks like a collapse.

The second is a bar chart of the product mix by share of revenue: five bars, one for each line, standing at 39.9%, 19.7%, 22.1%, 12.5% and 5.8%. The two charts answer different questions - the line chart answers 'is the business growing', the bar chart answers 'what is the business' - and a reader should be able to tell which is which from the titles alone.
bullets: Line chart: monthly revenue, twelve points, vertical axis 0 to J$2,100,000 in J$300,000 steps, labelled in J$ thousands to keep the labels readable.
Line chart - the fall into February is a fall of 10.2% on the month before, and the axis is left at zero so the size of the fall is honest.
Bar chart: share of revenue by product line - 39.9%, 19.7%, 22.1%, 12.5% and 5.8%, with the revenue in J$ printed at the end of each bar.
Both charts are printed in black and white with different patterns, so a reader without colour can still tell the bars apart.

pages.heading: Analysis and Discussion: the marketing mix, element by element
pages.body:
Product. The mix is sound in one respect and exposed in another. Bread, buns, patties and drops are everyday lines with dependable demand and 94.2% of revenue between them; the cake line is the one that grows with an occasion, and the June figures show it can carry a month. The weakness is variety: 60 customers asked for more variety only six times, but the two schools and the transport centre are exactly the market a wholemeal loaf or a small lunch pack would suit, and that is a gap rather than a complaint.

Price. The price check and the survey agree once they are read together. Marigold is the cheapest on the loaf that brings people through the door and dearer than both competitors on the patty that carries the second-largest contribution, and the mean value-for-money score of 3.42 is high in the middle and poor in the tail. The trial then prices the mistake in money: the two-for-500 promotion sold a quarter more patties and cost J$25,750 of contribution, so the recorded answer to a price complaint is that for this shop a price cut is the one promotional tool that does not work.

Place. The shop is on the busiest street in the town and 45.0% of the sample travels under a kilometre to reach it, so location is a strength rather than a problem. What is missing is the second half of place - the hours and the channels. The assistant's 'ten or twelve people a evening' turned away, the survey's 36.7% asking for later opening and the 55.0% who would use a phone order service all point the same way, and the evening trial then proves the point at the till.

Promotion. This is where the business is weakest and where the cheapest gain is. Word of mouth brought 45.0% of the sample, walking past brought 30.0%, and every paid channel together brought 25.0%. The shop has been relying on being found. The evening trial showed what a small, targeted promotion can do: J$11,000 of extra contribution in a fortnight for J$20,000 of cost, and no price cut.

pages.heading: Analysis and Discussion: SWOT drawn from the evidence
pages.body: The SWOT below is built only from figures that appear in this folder, and each entry names the table it came from. An entry that cannot be traced to evidence has been left out, which is why the threats column is shorter than the ones a textbook would print: the study found no evidence about the cost of flour over time, so it makes no claim about it.

table.caption: SWOT of Marigold Bakery, each entry traced to its evidence
rows: Bread, the daily line, is cheaper than the highway bakery: J$450 against J$480 (price check)
Every paid promotion channel together reaches only a quarter of the customers (survey: word of mouth 27, walked past 18)
Later opening: 27 of 60 customers asked for it (survey) and the trial earned J$11,000 a fortnight (trial)
The snackette sells patties at J$250 against Marigold's J$300 (price check)

pages.heading: Analysis and Discussion: judging the two promotions by their arithmetic
pages.body:
Two promotions were tested on the same shop in the same season, and the arithmetic separates them completely. The price promotion changed the price of one line by a sixth and produced 25.0% more patties; each of those extra patties carried J$55 of contribution instead of J$105, and the extra sales did not replace what the lower price took off the sales that would have happened anyway. The fortnight earned J$41,250 of contribution against J$63,000 with no promotion, and after J$4,000 of flyers the shop was J$25,750 worse off. That is the law of demand working exactly as the textbook says it should and a marketing decision failing anyway, because the question is never 'did more units sell' but 'did the shop keep more money'.

The evening trial changed no price at all. It changed the place element - the hours - and put a flyer in the hands of people already walking past. Every line rose by between 9.8% and 10.0% (the cake figure of 50.0% is on a base of only 6 orders and should not be read as a trend), contribution rose from J$256,000 to J$287,000, and after J$8,000 of flyers and J$12,000 of extra staff hours the fortnight was J$11,000 ahead. Repeated across a year at the same rate that is about J$286,000 of extra contribution, which is over half the annual fixed costs of the shop, and it needs no capital and no price change.
bullets: A price cut is a cost before it is anything else: the two-for-500 promotion gave away J$30,000 on the patties that would have sold at full price anyway.
The same fortnight proves the demand curve too: 25.0% more units at a lower price, which is what the syllabus predicts.
The evening trial is an example of the marketing mix being changed without touching price: place (hours) and promotion (flyers) only.
Contribution, not revenue, is the test: the evening fortnight added J$31,000 of revenue-earning contribution, of which J$20,000 went on the activity.
What the trial cannot say: whether customers keep coming late into September, or whether the flyers would work a second time.

pages.heading: Discussion: the numbers a lender, or the owner, would ask for
pages.body:
Recommendations that are not costed are wishes, so the four figures below are worked out from the same records as everything else. Contribution for the year was J$6,905,550 on revenue of J$21,460,000, so the contribution ratio is 32.2%: every J$100 of sales leaves about J$32 to pay the fixed costs and then to reward the owner. Fixed costs of J$5,520,000 a year divided by that ratio give a break-even revenue of J$17,154,202 - the point at which the shop pays for itself and earns nothing. Actual revenue was J$21,460,000, which leaves a margin of safety of 20.1%: sales could fall by a fifth before the shop made a loss.

Two consequences follow for the marketing plan. First, the shop is not in danger and does not need a rescue; it needs growth that can be paid for out of the contribution it already earns, which is why the recommendations avoid borrowing for a second oven. Second, a change worth J$11,000 a fortnight looks small against revenue of J$2,034,000 a month, but it is 2.4% of the monthly fixed costs, and a series of such changes is how a small business moves its break-even point.

pages.heading: Discussion: how reliable this evidence is, and what it cannot show
pages.body:
The evidence is strong in one direction and thin in another, and the difference should shape how the recommendations are read. It is strong about the shop's own trading: the sales record is complete for twelve months and the trial figures come from the till, so the contribution figures, the mix, the break-even point and the comparison between the two promotions are arithmetic on real (if invented) records. It is thinner about the market: 60 customers who mostly already buy at the shop, two competitor prices seen once, and competitor volumes that are interview estimates. Nothing in this project measures the town's total demand, and the estimated market share of 35.2% for bread must be read as an order of magnitude rather than a figure.

There is also an honest question about the trial itself. Two fortnights per change is long enough to see a difference in the till but not long enough to know whether a habit has formed, and the evening trial ran in a period whose weather has not been recorded. A candidate repeating this study would do three things differently: run each promotion for a full month, record the weather and the school calendar alongside the till, and survey the people who walk past without entering, which is the group this sample cannot reach. Those three changes would not alter the price-cut finding - the arithmetic of a J$50 cut on a J$105 contribution is what it is - but they would put the evening result on firmer ground.
bullets: Solid: twelve months of the firm's own sales; contribution, the ratio, break-even and the margin of safety all computed from it.
Solid: the two promotions were measured from the till in the same shop, same staff and same season.
Thin: the customer survey (60, mostly existing customers) cannot speak for the town.
Thin: competitor prices were checked once, and competitor volumes are interview estimates.
Unproven: whether a promotion changes the habit rather than the fortnight.
Missing altogether: the people who walk past the shop; their absence is a limit, not a small detail.

pages.heading: Conclusion and Recommendation: the aim answered
pages.body:
The aim was to find out how well the marketing of Marigold Bakery is working and what the owner should change, and the evidence answers it in four parts. The product mix is working: five lines earned J$21,460,000 of revenue and J$6,905,550 of contribution, and the bakery's bread is the cheapest on its street. The price is working on the daily line and not on the impulse line: value for money scored 3.42 out of 5, the lowest of the three ratings, and the price check shows why - Marigold is J$50 dearer than the snackette on the patty that customers buy at mid-morning. Promotion is the weak element: 45.0% of customers found the shop by word of mouth and 30.0% by walking past, so paid promotion has scarcely been tried. Place is the strongest opportunity, because the shop is in the right place and open at the wrong time: the assistant turns away ten or twelve people in the last hour, 45.0% of customers asked for later opening, and the trial proved that later hours earn J$11,000 a fortnight where a price cut lost J$25,750.

The answer to the second half of the aim, what to change, is therefore not 'advertise more' and certainly not 'cut prices'. It is to change the hours and the channels, and to leave the prices alone except where the price check shows the shop is out of line on the impulse lines.
bullets: Working well: the product mix (J$21,460,000 of revenue, J$6,905,550 of contribution) and the shop's location.
Working badly: promotion, where word of mouth and passing trade together found 75.0% of the customers.
Wrong tool, proved: a price cut. Two for 500 sold 25.0% more patties and lost J$25,750.
Right tool, proved: longer hours and flyers, J$11,000 gained in a fortnight with no price change.
Not proven: a delivery service. The survey shows demand (22 yes, 26 maybe) but no cost or route has been tested.

pages.heading: Conclusion and Recommendation: five recommendations, costed and ranked
pages.body: The recommendations are ranked by what they cost and what they earn, so that the owner can begin with the cheapest and let each one pay for the next. Every recommendation names the evidence it comes from, the person who would carry it out, the cost and the figure that would show within two terms whether it worked. Costs are the candidate's own estimates in Jamaican dollars and not quotations; the gains for the first two are taken from the trial and are stated at the same rate the trial produced.

pages.heading: Presentation: references, bibliography and the note on invented sources
pages.body: A real project would list the documents and people it used; because this sample is written for teaching, the business, the town and every record behind the tables are invented, and each one is tagged INVENTED below so that no reader mistakes it for evidence about a real firm. The method the references illustrate - name your sources, note the date you gathered each one, and never quote a business owner without saying who she is - is the part that transfers to a candidate's own project.
bullets: Marigold Bakery's sales record for the year July to June: the till roll and the cake order book, copied in week 1. INVENTED.
The customer questionnaire, 60 completed forms, printed in full in the appendix. INVENTED.
Interview with Mrs Ionie Clarke, owner, 12 March, 30 minutes, notes taken by hand and read back to her. INVENTED.
Interview with the representative of the flour distributor, 14 March, 20 minutes. INVENTED.
Interview with the shop assistant, 15 March, 20 minutes. INVENTED.
Price check sheet, one weekday morning, nine prices at three sellers, with the date and the time of day noted. INVENTED.
Promotion trial record: six weeks of till totals, kept on a single sheet so the three fortnights could be compared. INVENTED.

Method guidance followed: the six SBA sections and their marks as set out in the CSEC Compass Principles of Business guide used in class, and the class notes on the marketing mix, contribution, break-even and the margin of safety.

Syllabus concepts applied in the analysis: the marketing mix (product, price, place, promotion), the law of demand, contribution and the contribution ratio, break-even analysis, the margin of safety, SWOT analysis, and sole proprietorship as a form of business ownership.

pages.heading: Presentation: appendix - the questionnaire and the interview schedule
pages.body:
Marigold Bakery customer survey, Principles of Business SBA. Your answers are anonymous: no name or address is written on this form and the forms are only ever counted together. The study is a school project about how the bakery reaches its customers. Please answer for your household and hand the form back to the student. Thank you.

Part A of the form carries the ten closed questions below. Part B carried the three rating questions, each scored from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent). The interview schedule that follows was used with the owner, the supplier and the shop assistant, with the questions reordered for each speaker so that nobody was asked to comment on another person's job.
bullets: A1. How did you first hear about Marigold Bakery? (six options, one tick)
A2. How often do you buy here? (every day / three to five times a week / once or twice a week / less often)
A3. What do you buy most often? (bread / patties / buns / drops / cakes / other, written)
A4. What would make you buy more often? (later opening / lower prices / delivery / more variety / nothing)
A5. How far do you travel to the shop? (under 1 km / 1-3 km / over 3 km)
A6. Would you use an order-and-collect service by phone? (yes / maybe / no)
A7. Which age group are you in? (under 25 / 25-44 / 45-64 / 65 or over)
A8. Which of these have you ever bought elsewhere in Fairhaven? (bread / patties / buns / cakes / none)
A9. What time of day do you usually come? (morning / midday / evening)
A10. May we use your answer in the school project? (yes / no - only the yesses were kept)
B1-B3. Score the quality and freshness, the value for money, and the service out of five.

Interview schedule for the owner: how the prices are set; what is done to attract customers; what she would change if it cost nothing; what stops her changing it; how much a bag of flour costs and how many she buys.
Interview schedule for the supplier: how Marigold's orders compare with the other bakery's; whether both pay the same price; what happens to orders in the slow months.
Interview schedule for the shop assistant: what customers ask for and cannot get; what happens in the last hour; what people say about the prices; what she would change.

examinerNotes: The aim is cut into four research questions before any evidence is gathered, and each question names the instrument that answers it - which is why the project investigates the bakery rather than describing it.

Every number in the report is computed from one of four records, so a marker can check any figure: units multiplied by shelf price gives revenue, revenue less materials gives contribution, contribution less fixed costs gives profit, and fixed costs divided by the contribution ratio gives the break-even point.

The two promotions are judged by contribution rather than by units sold or revenue, which is the correct test and the one most candidates get wrong: the price cut sold 25.0% more patties and still lost J$25,750, while the evening hours earned J$11,000 without touching a price.
The analysis links the customer survey to the price check (price dissatisfaction concentrated on the patties that are dearer than the snackette) instead of reporting the two findings side by side.
The recommendations are ranked by cost against gain, each traces back to a named table, and each carries the figure that would show within two terms whether it worked.

The limitations are specific and consequential - 60 mostly existing customers, two-week promotions, estimated competitor volumes, and the people who walk past and are never sampled - and the market share is labelled estimated wherever it appears.
